Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

Virtual office address is NOT acceptable as the sole statutory registered office for an SL conducting regulated bunkering supply (ISIC 5222). The Commercial Registry and the competent Port Authority require a physical, accessible office in Spanish territory where corporate books, UBO documentation, insurance certificates and operating permits are kept. A virtual address may be used only as a supplementary commercial correspondence address after the physical registered office is proven.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central (name reservation) and Registro Mercantil Provincial of the provincial capital where the registered office is located; public deed executed before a Notario of the Colegio Notarial de España.

Governing statute

Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010, de 2 de julio, Texto Refundido de la Ley de Sociedades de Capital (LSC): arts. 19-24 (constitución), arts. 4 and 62 (minimum capital and full payment), arts. 22-39 (estatutos), arts. 209-230 (administration); Real Decreto 1784/1996, Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (RRM); Ley 14/2013 (apoyo a los emprendedores) enabling telematic incorporation via CIRCE; RDL 2/2011 for port service licensing.

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura pública de constitución (public incorporation deed), submitted for mandatory inscription (primera inscripción) in the Registro Mercantil; official tariffs comprise notarial arancel, registry arancel and name-certificate fee, variable by capital and region.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 27 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

EUR 3,000 minimum capital, fully subscribed and paid in cash before execution of the deed (LSC arts. 4 and 62); capital is deposited in a Spanish credit institution in the name of the company in formation and attested by a bank certificate (certificado de desembolso) annexed to the deed; no statutory escrow account is required. Sociedad de Formación Sucesiva exceptions apply only below EUR 3,000 with statutory reserve restrictions.

Funding & unlock path:

Paid-in capital rule: EUR 3,000 minimum capital, fully subscribed and paid in cash before execution of the deed (LSC arts. 4 and 62); capital is deposited in a Spanish credit institution in the name of the company in formation and attested by a bank certificate (certificado de desembolso) annexed to the deed; no statutory escrow account is required. Sociedad de Formación Sucesiva exceptions apply only below EUR 3,000 with statutory reserve restrictions.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT), including the Sede Electrónica de la AEAT at sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es. The competent tax administration is national, subject to specific regional tax arrangements not applicable to mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands.

E-government filing portal

A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada must obtain a provisional Número de Identificación Fiscal (NIF) from the AEAT after incorporation documentation is available and obtain the definitive NIF after registration details are completed. The application is generally made using Modelo 036, submitted electronically by an authorized representative or, where permitted, at an AEAT office. Required evidence normally includes the public deed of incorporation, Commercial Registry filing or registration evidence, articles of association, identification and powers of the legal representative, and identification of shareholders or beneficial owners when requested. Non-resident corporate shareholders generally require a Spanish NIF for tax identification and may need a representative or power of attorney for AEAT procedures. The Spanish NIF is also used as the VAT identification number, normally in the format ES plus the entity's NIF. Registration in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios through Modelo 036 is required for qualifying intra-EU transactions and inclusion in VIES. A foreign entity without a Spanish permanent establishment may obtain a Spanish NIF through its appointed representative or authorized agent where a Spanish tax filing, VAT obligation, customs operation, or other statutory tax procedure requires it. Customs Economic Operators Registration and Identification (EORI) registration is separately required for customs activity.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada must obtain a provisional Número de Identificación Fiscal (NIF) from the AEAT after incorporation documentation is available and obtain the definitive NIF after registration details are completed. The application is generally made using Modelo 036, submitted electronically by an authorized representative or, where permitted, at an AEAT office. Required evidence normally includes the public deed of incorporation, Commercial Registry filing or registration evidence, articles of association, identification and powers of the legal representative, and identification of shareholders or beneficial owners when requested. Non-resident corporate shareholders generally require a Spanish NIF for tax identification and may need a representative or power of attorney for AEAT procedures. The Spanish NIF is also used as the VAT identification number, normally in the format ES plus the entity's NIF. Registration in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios through Modelo 036 is required for qualifying intra-EU transactions and inclusion in VIES. A foreign entity without a Spanish permanent establishment may obtain a Spanish NIF through its appointed representative or authorized agent where a Spanish tax filing, VAT obligation, customs operation, or other statutory tax procedure requires it. Customs Economic Operators Registration and Identification (EORI) registration is separately required for customs activity.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

A Spanish SL is generally subject to Spanish Corporate Income Tax as a separate legal person and does not have a U.S.-style check-the-box election. Spanish tax-transparent treatment is limited to specific statutory structures and does not ordinarily apply to an SL. The entity may access statutory regimes where eligibility conditions are met, including the reduced regime for newly created entities, the regime for small entities, and qualifying special regimes such as the Canary Islands Zone regime, but these are not elective entity-classification elections. Spanish and EU anti-hybrid mismatch rules may deny deductions, include income, or otherwise neutralize mismatches involving related parties or structured arrangements. Tax consolidation and other special regimes require formal elections and statutory conditions.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general Spanish VAT registration threshold applies. A person carrying out an economic activity must register from the commencement of taxable economic activity or before the relevant taxable operations occur, regardless of turnover. The NIF and census registration are generally completed through Modelo 036. Separate registration may be required for intra-EU transactions, distance sales, importation, customs activity, or special regimes.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods dispatched or transported from Spanish VAT territory to a destination outside the EU may qualify for VAT exemption with the right to deduct input VAT under Article 21 of the Spanish VAT Law, provided the supplier, purchaser, transport, and documentary evidence requirements are satisfied and the goods actually leave the VAT territory. Supplies to qualifying vessels used for navigation on the high seas and for specified commercial, industrial, or fishing activities, including qualifying fuel and provisions, may qualify for the specific vessel-related exemption under Article 22, subject to vessel status, use, delivery, and documentary conditions; bunker fuel is not automatically exempt merely because it is delivered to a ship. Intra-EU supplies require the applicable exemption conditions, including a valid customer VAT number, transport to another Member State, and correct EC Sales List reporting. Services are generally governed by place-of-supply rules rather than a blanket export zero rate. Bunkering, storage, delivery, and related logistics services must be analysed separately, including the special rules for services connected with immovable property, transport, vessels, and intermediary services where relevant. Input VAT refunds require valid invoices, accounting records, proof of taxable business activity, and filing through the applicable domestic or non-established-business refund procedure.

  • Electronic export customs declaration accepted by Spanish Customs, including the Movement Reference Number (MRN)
  • Electronic confirmation of exit or equivalent customs proof that the goods physically left the EU customs and VAT territory
  • Commercial invoice identifying the supplier, customer, goods, quantity, value, VAT treatment, and relevant vessel or delivery details
  • Bill of lading, sea waybill, bunker delivery note, delivery receipt, or equivalent transport and receipt evidence identifying the vessel and delivered fuel or lubricants
  • Purchase order, contract, and evidence of the customer's entitlement to any vessel-related VAT exemption
  • Evidence of the vessel's registration, activity, and qualifying commercial, industrial, fishing, or navigation status where Article 22 exemption is claimed
  • Inventory, loading, meter, quantity, and custody records reconciling the invoiced products with the physically delivered products
  • Supplier accounting records, VAT return entries, and EC Sales List records where an intra-EU transaction is involved
  • Bank payment evidence and, where applicable, documentary evidence supporting the economic substance of the transaction and any VAT refund claim

Spain does not currently operate a universal real-time pre-clearance system for every VAT invoice. The Immediate Supply of Information (Suministro Inmediato de Información, SII) requires qualifying taxpayers, including entities exceeding the statutory turnover threshold, VAT groups, and entities that opt into the system, to electronically submit specified invoice-record data to the AEAT, generally within statutory short filing periods. Royal Decree 1007/2023 establishes requirements for computerised invoicing and billing systems, including integrity, traceability, preservation, event logging, and, under the VERI*FACTU model, transmission of invoice records to the AEAT; implementation dates are subject to the applicable transitional rules and subsequent regulatory timetable. Business-to-business electronic invoicing under the Law on the Creation and Growth of Companies is being phased in through implementing regulations and is not equivalent to universal prior VAT clearance. Electronic invoices must satisfy Spanish and EU invoicing, authenticity, integrity, legibility, storage, and audit-access requirements. Customs electronic declarations and MRN-based export procedures apply to goods exports.

Spain has no general rule requiring export proceeds to be repatriated within 180 days as a condition for VAT zero-rating or export exemption. The taxpayer must instead prove the taxable treatment and actual export or qualifying vessel supply within the statutory record-retention and assessment periods. If the exemption is unsupported or the goods did not leave the relevant territory, the AEAT may assess the unpaid VAT, late-payment interest, and penalties, and may deny or claw back related input VAT refunds. Under the General Tax Law, inaccurate or incomplete tax returns may generally attract penalties based on the unpaid or improperly refunded amount, commonly ranging from 50% to 150% depending on severity, concealment, fraud, repeated conduct, and the resulting tax loss; unjustified refunds and fraudulent documentation may trigger additional consequences. Customs infringements may lead to customs debt, recovery of duties and taxes, seizure or forfeiture measures, and administrative penalties under EU and Spanish customs law. Intentional tax fraud can constitute a criminal tax offence where the statutory thresholds and other Penal Code conditions are met, including the general tax-loss threshold of EUR 120,000 per tax and assessment period. Related-party, carousel-fraud, false-documentation, and fuel-diversion indicators receive heightened audit scrutiny.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain is a Eurozone member; the euro is fully convertible. Current account transactions (including trade in goods and services, dividends, and interest) are unrestricted. Capital account transactions (e.g., foreign direct investment, portfolio investment) are also liberalized, but require post-transaction statistical declaration to the Banco de España for amounts exceeding €1,000,000 or when the transaction involves tax havens. Profit remittance is unrestricted, subject to corporate income tax (25% standard rate) and potential withholding tax on dividends (19% for EU residents, 0% under certain EU directives). No exchange control approval is required for remittances, but banks must verify the underlying transaction and report to the authorities.

Export proceeds surrender rules

There is no mandatory surrender of export proceeds in Spain. Exporters may retain foreign currency in non-resident or resident foreign currency accounts. However, all export transactions must be declared to the Banco de España for statistical purposes within 30 days of the transaction if the amount exceeds EUR 12,500 (or equivalent). For bunkering services, the export of goods (fuel) is treated as a service under the ISIC code; the same reporting thresholds apply. No mandatory conversion ratio exists; the exporter may choose to convert to EUR or hold foreign currency.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain) in coordination with the Dirección General de Comercio Internacional e Inversiones (DGCI) under the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Tourism; the Spanish Foreign Exchange Regulation is governed by Royal Decree 1816/1991 and subsequent amendments.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Revolut Fit: High

Feasibility rating: Medium. Spain recognizes Electronic Money Institutions (EMIs) under the Payment Services Directive (PSD2) and the E-Money Directive. Licensed EMIs (e.g., Bnext, N26, Revolut) can provide multi-currency accounts and cross-border payment services. However, for bunkering operations involving large-value trade settlements and standby letters of credit, traditional banks are preferred due to their ability to issue and confirm LCs. EMIs may face restrictions on providing credit or issuing guarantees. Legal constraints: EMIs must be authorized by the Banco de España or passported from another EU state; they are subject to AML/KYC obligations but may not offer full treasury services. For high-risk sectors like marine fuel supply, EMIs may impose enhanced due diligence or decline onboarding.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

High-risk industry classification (ISIC 5222 – Marine bunkering) due to potential for sanctions evasion, smuggling, or money laundering via fuel trade.

Root cause: High-risk industry classification (ISIC 5222 – Marine bunkering) due to potential for sanctions evasion, smuggling, or money laundering via fuel trade.

Defense evidence: Provide: (1) Valid bunkering license issued by the Spanish Port Authority (Puertos del Estado) or regional port authority; (2) Detailed business plan and client list with due diligence on counterparties; (3) Evidence of compliance with international sanctions (e.g., OFAC, EU sanctions) through screening software; (4) Financial statements and proof of source of funds for initial capital; (5) Contracts with suppliers and buyers, including Incoterms and payment terms; (6) Tax registration certificates (CIF/NIF) and corporate registry extract; (7) Beneficial ownership declaration (UBO) with supporting documentation; (8) Any existing bank references or letters of credit from reputable institutions.
Non-resident ownership structure with complex corporate chain (e.g., offshore entities) triggering enhanced due diligence.

Root cause: Non-resident ownership structure with complex corporate chain (e.g., offshore entities) triggering enhanced due diligence.

Defense evidence: Provide: (1) Full corporate structure chart with ownership percentages; (2) Legal opinion from a recognized law firm confirming the legitimacy of the structure; (3) Copies of passports and proof of address for all UBOs; (4) Business rationale for the structure (e.g., tax efficiency, operational presence); (5) Evidence of substance in Spain (e.g., office lease, local staff, bank account activity); (6) Regulatory filings (e.g., annual accounts) for all entities in the chain.
High transaction volumes or unusual payment patterns (e.g., rapid in/out flows) typical of bunkering operations.

Root cause: High transaction volumes or unusual payment patterns (e.g., rapid in/out flows) typical of bunkering operations.

Defense evidence: Provide: (1) Detailed cash flow projections and historical transaction records; (2) Contracts and invoices for each transaction; (3) Bill of lading and delivery receipts for fuel; (4) Explanation of the commercial cycle (e.g., purchase from refinery, sale to ship); (5) Compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) internal controls, including transaction monitoring procedures; (6) Appointment of a compliance officer and AML training certificates.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Compliant wire transfer protocols: Inbound capital injections (e.g., equity contributions from non-resident shareholders) must be routed via SWIFT MT103 with proper purpose codes. For equity injection, use purpose code 'P01' (Foreign Direct Investment) or 'P02' (Capital increase) as per Banco de España's statistical classification. The transfer must be accompanied by a notarized board resolution and updated corporate registry filing. Verification: The bank will require the underlying documentation (e.g., share subscription agreement, capital increase deed) and may report to the Banco de España. For loans from shareholders, use purpose code 'P03' (Financial loans) and ensure compliance with thin capitalization rules (30% EBITDA limit). The funds must be received in EUR or convertible currency; if in foreign currency, the bank will convert at market rate.Clearing rails for trade settlements: For bunkering operations, outbound payments to fuel suppliers and port authorities are typically executed via SWIFT MT103 (wire transfer) for direct payments, or via Commercial Letters of Credit (LC) for larger, deferred payments. Standby LCs are used as guarantees for performance or payment. The bank will require underlying contracts and invoices. For payments to non-EU suppliers, ensure compliance with EU sanctions and export controls. For intra-EU payments, SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) transfers are efficient, but for non-EUR currencies, SWIFT is necessary. The bank may offer trade finance products such as documentary collections (D/P, D/A) and supply chain finance.FX Forwards: Standard OTC forward contracts with maturities up to 12 months, available from major Spanish banks. No exchange control restrictions; contracts must be documented under ISDA or local master agreements.Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs): Permissible for currencies with limited convertibility (e.g., certain Latin American currencies) but rarely used for EUR/USD or EUR/GBP. For bunkering, if trading with non-EUR currencies, NDFs may be used for hedging exposure to exotic currencies.Currency Swaps: Cross-currency interest rate swaps (CCIRS) are permissible for long-term hedging of principal and interest payments. Banks require a credit line and collateral. For bunkering, short-term FX swaps (swap de divisas) are common to manage liquidity in different currencies.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Feasibility rating: Medium. Spain recognizes Electronic Money Institutions (EMIs) under the Payment Services Directive (PSD2) and the E-Money Directive. Licensed EMIs (e.g., Bnext, N26, Revolut) can provide multi-currency accounts and cross-border payment services. However, for bunkering operations involving large-value trade settlements and standby letters of credit, traditional banks are preferred due to their ability to issue and confirm LCs. EMIs may face restrictions on providing credit or issuing guarantees. Legal constraints: EMIs must be authorized by the Banco de España or passported from another EU state; they are subject to AML/KYC obligations but may not offer full treasury services. For high-risk sectors like marine fuel supply, EMIs may impose enhanced due diligence or decline onboarding.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% standard Spanish Corporate Income Tax rate. Newly created entities and entities qualifying as startups may generally apply a 15% rate for the first profitable tax period and the immediately following period, subject to statutory conditions and exclusions.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax on dividends paid by a Spanish SL to a non-resident, subject to domestic exemptions and treaty relief. The EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive exemption may apply through Spanish implementation where the parent is a qualifying EU or qualifying EEA company, the minimum participation and holding-period conditions are satisfied, the anti-abuse requirements are met, and the recipient is subject to a qualifying tax. A 5% participation threshold and a minimum one-year holding requirement generally apply, with statutory alternatives for completing the holding period.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Modelo 200 is generally due within the 25 calendar days following the six months after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year taxpayer, the normal filing period is 1 to 25 July, with the payment-direct-debit deadline generally earlier. Modelo 202 is generally due from 1 to 20 April, October, and December. Modelo 232 is generally due during the month following the ten-month period after the tax period ends; for a 31 December year-end, this is normally November. If the final day is not a business day, the applicable electronic filing and payment rules extend the deadline to the next business day.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Spain does not use one universal monetary threshold for all mandatory local-file and master-file obligations. Full transfer-pricing documentation generally applies to material related-party transactions, subject to statutory simplified-documentation rules. Documentation is generally not required for transactions with the same related party that do not exceed EUR 250,000 in aggregate for the tax period under the same valuation method, subject to exclusions. A master file is generally relevant for Spanish entities belonging to a group required to prepare consolidated accounts, particularly where consolidated group turnover reaches EUR 750 million for Country-by-Country Reporting purposes. Modelo 232 is generally triggered by transaction-category thresholds, including transactions of the same type and method exceeding EUR 250,000, specific transactions exceeding EUR 100,000 in certain tax-haven categories, or related-party transactions exceeding 50% of the entity's turnover, subject to the current form instructions.

Economic substance scope: Spain does not operate a separate UAE-style Economic Substance Regulations regime. Substance is nevertheless material under Spanish transfer-pricing rules, the beneficial-ownership and EU exemption rules, the General Anti-Abuse Rule, the anti-tax-avoidance rule, controlled foreign company rules, interest limitation rules, treaty principal-purpose tests, and deductibility requirements. A Spanish bunkering SL should maintain real operational capacity proportionate to its business, including personnel or outsourced operational control, port and fuel-supply contracts, inventory and delivery records, risk control, banking activity, accounting records, decision-making evidence, and commercial rationale. A conduit entity receiving dividends, royalties, interest, or service fees without functions, assets, risks, or decision-making authority faces denial of relief, income recharacterization, withholding assessments, and penalties.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate Income Tax evasion and fraudulent accounting

Statutory sanction: Administrative penalties may generally range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax, with repayment of tax and interest. Tax fraud becomes a criminal offense where the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 for a tax period and tax, interest, and criminal fines apply. Ordinary tax fraud may carry imprisonment of one to five years and a fine of one to six times the amount defrauded; aggravated cases may carry two to six years' imprisonment and a fine of two to six times the amount defrauded.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers may incur civil liability to the company, tax liability as collaborating or subsidiarily liable persons, disqualification consequences, asset seizure, and criminal liability. Imprisonment is possible in qualifying criminal cases. Travel restrictions may be imposed by a court where necessary to secure criminal proceedings; there is no automatic travel ban for ordinary tax arrears.
VAT fraud and excise-duty fraud

Statutory sanction: Recovery of unpaid VAT and excise duties, late-payment interest, administrative penalties, seizure or forfeiture of fuel and equipment, suspension or loss of excise authorizations, and potential criminal prosecution where statutory thresholds or organized-fraud conditions are met.

Director personal liability: Directors who authorize or knowingly facilitate fraudulent VAT or excise arrangements may face joint or subsidiary tax liability, civil restitution, administrative disqualification, asset seizure, and imprisonment in criminal cases.
Transfer-pricing manipulation

Statutory sanction: The AEAT may make a primary adjustment, impose secondary adjustments, deny deductions, assess withholding tax, and impose transfer-pricing documentation or valuation penalties. Documentation-related penalties may be fixed or calculated by reference to the undeclared or incorrectly valued amounts under the Corporate Income Tax Law.

Director personal liability: Directors may be liable where the conduct is intentional, negligent, or part of a tax-fraud scheme. Criminal exposure arises if the resulting tax fraud exceeds the criminal threshold or forms part of falsification, money laundering, or organized fraud.
Beneficial-ownership, treaty-shopping, and conduit-company abuse

Statutory sanction: Denial of treaty or domestic exemption, withholding at the full domestic rate, payment of arrears and interest, General Anti-Abuse Rule assessments, and penalties for incorrect withholding or reporting.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur withholding-agent liability and civil restitution obligations. Intentional participation in sham arrangements may create criminal tax-fraud or document-fraud exposure.
Money laundering and AML failure

Statutory sanction: Under Spanish AML legislation, serious and very serious breaches may result in public or private reprimands, fines that can reach the higher of statutory fixed amounts or a percentage of the transaction or annual turnover, temporary management or activity prohibitions, and loss of authorization. Criminal money laundering may carry imprisonment generally from six months to six years and fines from one to three times the value of the assets, with aggravated consequences in specified cases.

Director personal liability: Managers, compliance officers, and directors may be personally fined, disqualified, and prosecuted where they knowingly participate in or negligently permit laundering. Asset freezing, confiscation, civil restitution, and court-ordered travel restrictions may apply.
Sanctions, export controls, and restricted-party dealings

Statutory sanction: EU and Spanish sanctions may impose asset freezes, prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, administrative fines, authorization loss, contract invalidity, and criminal liability under applicable implementing legislation.

Director personal liability: Directors and compliance personnel who authorize or knowingly facilitate prohibited transactions may face personal administrative and criminal liability, confiscation, civil damages, and court-ordered restrictions.
Unlicensed bunkering, port, environmental, or fuel-quality operations

Statutory sanction: Potential consequences include administrative fines, suspension or revocation of licenses, detention of vessels, seizure of fuel, cleanup and remediation costs, environmental liability, civil claims, and criminal prosecution for serious pollution or safety offenses.

Director personal liability: Directors may face civil environmental liability, administrative liability, and criminal prosecution where they ordered, knowingly tolerated, or negligently failed to prevent the unlawful operation. Courts may impose restitution, confiscation, and restrictions on management activity.
Failure to retain records and file statutory information

Statutory sanction: Fixed or percentage-based penalties may apply for failure to file, incomplete or inaccurate information, obstruction, deficient accounting, withholding failures, and transfer-pricing documentation failures. Assessments may include tax, interest, and denial of deductions.

Director personal liability: The SL's directors may be secondarily liable for tax debts where statutory conditions for administrator liability are met, especially after repeated non-compliance or dissolution without satisfying creditors. Civil claims, disqualification, and criminal exposure may follow where concealment or falsification is involved.
Asset stripping and improper profit repatriation

Statutory sanction: Repayment of unlawful distributions, creditor claims, insolvency clawback, director liability, tax adjustments, withholding assessments, and possible insolvency or fraud offenses.

Director personal liability: Directors may owe civil restitution, creditor compensation, and insolvency-related damages; may be disqualified from management; and may face criminal liability for fraudulent insolvency, misappropriation, or creditor prejudice. Travel restrictions are court-dependent and not automatic.
